lesson.title: Networks: getting the data home
lesson.subtitle: Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, mobile or LoRa, and when to pass it on

video.title: Networks: getting the data home
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph at the office window, pointing up at a water tank on a far hill; a Wi-Fi symbol fades out at the staffroom door.
scenes.animation: Wi-Fi rings shrink and stop short of the hill.
scenes.narration: Our water tank sensor works perfectly. But the tank is up a hill, four hundred metres from the office, and our Wi-Fi stops at the staffroom door. So nobody knows when it's nearly empty.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: networks, and how a sensor's data gets home.

scenes.visual: Four question cards pinned on a board: a map pin, a battery, a data stack, a banknote.
scenes.animation: Cards pin up one by one.
scenes.narration: Every network is a trade-off, so ask four questions. How far? How much power? How much data, and how often? And what will it cost each month?

scenes.visual: A phone picking up a nearby sensor; a router on the staffroom wall with its range drawn as a circle.
scenes.animation: Two range circles grow and stop.
scenes.narration: Bluetooth Low Energy reaches ten to thirty metres, usually to a phone, on very little power. Wi-Fi carries lots of data, but only thirty to fifty metres indoors, and needs a router with power.

scenes.visual: A mobile mast over a village; a LoRa sensor on a farm sending a tiny packet kilometres away.
scenes.animation: A small packet hops across the fields.
scenes.narration: A mobile network works wherever there's coverage, but each sensor needs a SIM and a monthly plan. LoRa is made for sensors: two to five kilometres in town, ten or more in open country, on very little power, but only a few dozen bytes at a time.

scenes.visual: A pupil takes a memory card out of a logger box by the garden and carries it to the computer room.
scenes.animation: The card travels across the school map.
scenes.narration: Sometimes the best network is no radio at all. A logger saves to a memory card, and a pupil collects it weekly: no signal, no bill.

scenes.visual: Amina at the foot of the hill, looking up at the tank. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! The tank is four hundred metres away, up a hill, with no power or Wi-Fi. Which network fits best?

scenes.visual: The tank sensor sends a small packet down the hill to a gateway box on the office roof.
scenes.animation: The packet arcs down; the gateway's light blinks.
scenes.narration: LoRa. Four hundred metres is easy for LoRa, but far beyond Bluetooth and Wi-Fi. A water level is a few bytes, the sensor can run for years on batteries, and one gateway can hear sensors all over the school.

scenes.visual: A chain: the tank sensor, the gateway on the roof, a cloud, the caretaker's phone buzzing.
scenes.animation: A reading travels the chain; the phone lights up.
scenes.narration: A gateway is the bridge between the sensors' radio and the internet. It hears their messages and passes them on, over Wi-Fi, a cable or the mobile network, to a computer or a phone.

scenes.visual: Sensors scattered over a farm; a message hops from the farthest one through neighbours to the gateway. One node breaks; the message takes another path.
scenes.animation: A packet hops node to node; a node turns grey and the route bends round it.
scenes.on_screen_text: Out of reach? Pass it on
scenes.narration: What if a sensor is out of reach? In a mesh, sensors pass messages hop by hop, each to a neighbour in range, until one reaches the gateway. If one fails, the message can often go another way.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah with a garden map: a far sensor, a middle sensor and the gateway, with range circles. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A sensor at the far end of the garden can't reach the gateway, but a sensor halfway can reach both. What's the cheapest fix?

scenes.visual: Four icons line up: a map pin, a phone, a LoRa antenna, a chain of hops.
scenes.animation: Icons line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Let the halfway sensor pass the messages on: in a mesh, they hop to the gateway. Remember: weigh distance, power, data and cost; Bluetooth or Wi-Fi when it's near, LoRa and a gateway when it's far, and hops to cross the gaps.

scenes.visual: Pupils spread across the playground with arms out; a folded note passes hand to hand towards a pupil wearing a 'gateway' sign.
scenes.animation: The note hops pupil to pupil; one pupil steps out and the note goes round.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: the playground radio game. One pupil is the gateway, and notes pass only to someone within arm's reach. Who gets cut off? Add a relay, then take one pupil away and find another route.

checkpoints.prompt: 400 m up a hill, no power or Wi-Fi, a water level every 15 minutes. Which network?

options.text: LoRa, with a gateway at school

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — 400 m is far beyond Bluetooth and Wi-Fi but easy for LoRa, and a water level is only a few bytes.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — Bluetooth and Wi-Fi reach tens of metres, not 400. LoRa reaches kilometres on little power, and a water level is tiny.

checkpoints.prompt: The far sensor can't reach the gateway, but a sensor halfway reaches both. Cheapest fix?

options.text: Let the halfway sensor pass them on

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the halfway sensor can relay its messages hop by hop, with no new hardware.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — sending more often doesn't add range. Let the halfway sensor relay the messages: that's a mesh.
